hints: Look at which way the path bends in Fig. 7.1 and remember a $\beta^-$ particle is negatively charged, so the force on it acts opposite to the field direction.
walkthrough:
**Link bending to force**
You can see the $\beta^-$ particle bends upwards once inside the field. That tells you the electric force $F$ on it must have an upward component.

**Use the negative charge**
For any charge, $$F = qE$$ in vector terms. A $\beta^-$ particle is an electron with charge $q = -e$, so force is opposite to field. To get an upward force, the field $E$ must point downwards. So draw a downward arrow inside the shaded region.
Final answer: Electric field arrow points vertically downwards in the plane of the paper, opposite to the upward deflection.

hints: Start by identifying what a $\beta^-$ particle is and what mass to use, and notice the kinetic energy is given in eV not in SI units.
Think about how kinetic energy is linked to mass and speed for a particle moving much slower than light.
Remember to first convert $460\text{ eV}$ to joules using $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$, then rearrange for $v$ before substituting numbers.
walkthrough:
**Identify the particle and energy**
A $\beta^-$ particle is a fast electron, so $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$. Its kinetic energy is given as $460\text{ eV}$. Electronvolts must be changed to joules for use with $m$ in kg.

**Rearrange kinetic energy for speed**
For non-relativistic motion: $$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2E_k}{m}}$$ $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 7.36 \times 10^{-17}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}}$$ $$v = 1.3 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ to 2 s.f. This is well below the speed of light, so the classical formula is fine.

hints: Recall what you know about $\beta^-$ decay - do all emitted electrons share the total decay energy in the same way, or is the energy shared with another particle?
Think about how a faster or slower particle entering the same transverse field would be deflected differently because of the time spent in the field.
walkthrough:
**Remember beta energies are not all the same**
In $\beta^-$ decay the available energy is shared randomly between the $\beta$ particle and an antineutrino. That gives a continuous spectrum of kinetic energies, not a single value. So other particles will have different speeds from $1.3 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

**Link speed to path in the field**
The transverse deflection depends on the acceleration $a = F/m = eE/m$ and the time spent in the field, which depends on entry speed. A slower particle spends longer in the field and deflects more, a faster one deflects less. Therefore with various speeds they follow different curved paths.

Final answer: No, they will not follow the same path. $\beta^-$ particles from the same source have a range of kinetic energies and speeds, so they experience the electric force for different times and are deflected by different amounts.
